prompt: You're a senior engineer who has spent years watching how big tech companies hire and promote people, and you've long been a baseball stats nerd on the side. Write an essay on how organizations misjudge talent: what goes wrong when people trust their gut about who is good, and what that implies for hiring and promotion in software.
Sports teams took forever to accept stats over scouts' gut feelings. Should that make us more or less confident that tech companies are good at judging engineering talent?
When engineers at your company talk about who the 'great' engineers are, do they actually agree? What are they really basing it on?
Why do caches seem to show up in so many big outages? Conceptually a cache is about the simplest service there is, so what makes it so failure-prone in a large distributed system?
Can someone explain how CFS CPU quotas actually work for containers, and why a service with lots of threads gets throttled even when its average CPU usage is well under its limit?
Everyone says to size thread pools at 2x the number of cores. Is that actually good advice for services running in CPU-limited containers?
